candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the HTML fragment passed to the cleaner (e.g. a stored comment/post rendered with Jsoup.clean). Example shape:
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Default/canned whitelists (Whitelist.none/simpleText/basic/basicWithImages/relaxed — Whitelist.java:76-180) do not contain `noscript`, so default Jsoup.clean usage is not affected; with noscript absent the tag is dropped, children are promoted into the destination and the `` stays inside a quoted attribute value that jsoup escapes, so the browser cannot break out. I also checked that: text nodes are escaped (TextNode.java:92-99); quotes and ampersands are escaped in attribute values (Entities.java:111-137); URL attributes are protocol-checked via Whitelist.testValidProtocol/Node.absUrl, and the raw-value fallback there rejects javascript:/data: values; DataNode raw output (DataNode.java:42-44) only concerns whitelisted script/style parents by design; tags/attribute names that reach the output are constrained to whitelist-registered names. The remaining gap is precisely the scripting-flag divergence for noscript, which the code itself flags ('if scripting enabled, rawtext', HtmlTreeBuilder.java:77/HtmlTreeBuilderState.java:507).
candidates.impact: Cross-site scripting in the consuming web application: a script-capable handler (onerror/onload etc.) authored inside what the sanitizer believed was an inert attribute value becomes executable markup after the browser reparses the cleaned fragment. Impact is limited to deployments whose whitelist includes `noscript` (a plausible extension, since the Whitelist API explicitly invites adding tags and nothing in the API/code warns about noscript's scripting-flag-dependent parsing).
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The application's Whitelist must allow the `noscript` tag (Whitelist.addTags("noscript") or equivalent; the canned whitelists none/simpleText/basic/basicWithImages/relaxed do NOT include it). 2) The payload needs at least one attribute that is allowed on a whitelisted element inside the noscript (e.g. `title` on `a` via Whitelist.relaxed(), which has no protocol entry for title so the value passes through unchecked). 3) The sanitized output must be inserted into a page parsed with scripting enabled (the normal case), i.e. the app must use the cleaned string as HTML.
candidates.root_cause: The HTML parser has no scripting flag: noscript content is always parsed as markup (HtmlTreeBuilderState.java:122-125 inserts noscript and switches to InHeadNoscript; InBody treats noscript as an ordinary element; HtmlTreeBuilder.java:76-77 documents 'if scripting enabled, rawtext'), whereas browsers with scripting enabled parse the same mark-up as RAWTEXT. The Cleaner (Cleaner.java:85-117) then copies whitelisted elements/attributes verbatim with only value-level escaping, and attribute serialization escapes '"' and '&' but deliberately leaves '<', '>' and '/' unescaped (Attribute.java:82-89 with Entities.java:120-131). The result is output in which a markup sequence that jsoup treated as an attribute value is reinterpreted by the browser as live markup once a whitelisted <noscript> wrapper puts it back into a raw-text context.
candidates.title: Cleaner mutation XSS via `<noscript>` (parsed as markup by jsoup, as raw text by browsers with scripting enabled)
candidates.trace: 1) Parsing: tokeniser Data state → `". 4) Re-parse by the consumer: a browser with scripting enabled enters RAWTEXT for `
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no execution, tests or browser was used (prohibited in this run), and the snapshot contains no test sources. I could not verify against upstream/git history whether this divergence was later fixed, and I cannot observe the actual whitelist a consuming application uses. Whether a given deployment is affected depends on its whitelist allowing `noscript` and on an allowed attribute being present in the payload.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 / mutation XSS (sanitizer bypass through parser differential)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 60 model-visible files, all under src/main (Java sources for org.jsoup.nodes, parser, safety, select, helper, examples) plus pom.xml, .travis.yml, .gitignore and src/main/javadoc/overview.html; binary/NUL-containing files are skipped by the tooling (none were flagged). Relation index: 60/60 files indexed, 0 hash mismatches, 0 missing files, 1604 symbols / 5147 edges / 30 facts; no build, tests or SAST oracle were loaded or run. I read in full or in relevant part: CharacterReader, Tokeniser, TokeniserState, Token, Tag, TokenQueue, TreeBuilder, HtmlTreeBuilder, HtmlTreeBuilderState, XmlTreeBuilder, Parser; Node, Element, Document, Attribute, Attributes, TextNode, DataNode, Comment, DocumentType, XmlDeclaration, Entities, FormElement; Cleaner, Whitelist; DataUtil, HttpConnection, StringUtil, W3CDom, Validate; and I sampled Evaluator/Elements/Selector-adjacent code. Not reviewed line-by-line: the bulk of Evaluator/QueryParser/Selector/StructuralEvaluator/CombiningEvaluator/Elements bodies, the Connection interface beyond security-relevant javadoc, DescendableLinkedList, the example classes, and ParseError/ParseErrorList. There are no test sources in this snapshot, so no repository tests could be used as corroboration.
limitations: Static, read-only review: no code was executed, no unit tests, scanners, fuzzing or browser were used, so no finding is runtime-confirmed (the candidate is a lead only).

The P1 relation index is navigational only (syntactic call/containment hints); it does not prove reachability or data flow, and unresolved call sites (e.g. HashMap/Charset/URL APIs) had to be judged from source text.

I could not diff this snapshot against upstream jsoup or any patch/changelog (external lookups prohibited), so statements about 'upstream behaviour' are recalled reasoning, not verified evidence; version identity comes from pom.xml (1.8.3-SNAPSHOT).

Exploitability of the submitted candidate depends on deployment configuration that is not present in this repository (whether the application's Whitelist includes `noscript` and which attributes it allows), and on the consumer rendering the cleaned string as HTML with scripting enabled.
Parser/tree-builder DoS properties (super-linear behaviour, resource growth) were reasoned about statically; I could not measure time/memory, so those leads remain unconfirmed.

Coverage of select/* and the Connection interface API surface was by reading of security-relevant paths and spot checks rather than exhaustive review; any issue confined to query parsing or callback plumbing may have been missed.

rejected_leads.lead: Quadratic CPU consumption in RcdataLessthanSign: for `<title>`/`<textarea>` content the tokeniser calls CharacterReader.containsIgnoreCase("</"+appropriateEndTagName) for each '<'+letter while remaining in RCDATA (TokeniserState.java:216-233, CharacterReader.java:327-332), each call scanning the remainder of the input — so input such as `<textarea>` + many "<a" pairs + a final `</textarea>` costs O(n^2) work
rejected_leads.reason: Real super-linear behaviour is derivable from the code, but I could not turn it into a definite termination-failure or a concrete bounded cost without executing measurements, and I could not establish that this is the intended (or a reported) issue. Kept as an unconfirmed performance/DoS lead, not submitted as the candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Cleaner copies DataNode content unescaped when the parent tag is whitelisted (Cleaner.java:103, DataNode.java:42-44): a whitelist that allows `script`/`style` yields verbatim, unescaped script/CSS in the cleaned output
rejected_leads.reason: Correctness feature rather than a hidden flaw: DataNode parents can only be script/style, and whitelisting script/style (or event handlers) is inherently unsafe and explicitly warned about in Whitelist's javadoc (Whitelist.java:56-60). Not a distinct root cause from the candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: HttpConnection forwards request cookies on redirects to a different origin and also copies each response's cookies into the follow-up request (HttpConnection.java:522-534, 638-642)
rejected_leads.reason: Credential-leakage-flavoured, but the behaviour is consistent with the library's documented 'simplified cookie model' (Connection.java:365-374), cookies are only sent when the caller sets them, and there is no attacker-controlled input reaching the sink without the application deliberately adding cookies/redirect-following. Design limitation, not a supported vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Cleaner.isValid NPEs when the dirty document has no body (frameset documents): copySafeNodes is called without the null guard used in clean() (Cleaner.java:64-70 vs 43-51)
rejected_leads.reason: Null-pointer/robustness bug with no attacker-controlled privilege or data impact beyond an unchecked exception; below the candidate threshold.

rejected_leads.lead: TokeniserState.RcdataLessthanSign line 227 performs r.unconsume() before switching to Data, which differs from what I recalled of the upstream divergence-from-spec branch
rejected_leads.reason: Even if this is a local deviation, the effect is to re-tokenise the '<' as a start tag (closer to the HTML spec) and I found no sanitizer consequence: the serialized output still escapes text/attribute values, so it does not create a bypass on its own.

summary: Reviewed the jsoup 1.8.3-SNAPSHOT sources (60 files: org.jsoup nodes/parser/safety/select/helper + examples, pom.xml, .travis.yml, javadoc overview). I traced the sanitizer path end-to-end (Jsoup.clean → Cleaner.CleaningVisitor → Whitelist.isSafeAttribute/testValidProtocol → Element/Attribute/Entities serialization) and the parser states that decide what is text vs markup (Data/Rcdata/Rawtext/ScriptData/Cdata, InHead/InHeadNoscript/InBody/Text). The strongest source-supported issue is a mutation-XSS (mXSS) failure of the Cleaner around `<noscript>`: jsoup parses noscript content as ordinary markup (scripting-disabled semantics), the Cleaner/serializer can re-emit that content inside a quoted attribute value, and a browser with scripting enabled reparses the sanitized fragment in RAWTEXT mode for noscript, turning the previously-quoted bytes into live markup. This requires the consuming whitelist to allow `noscript` (the canned whitelists do not), so it is a lead with a configuration prerequisite, not a default-configuration bypass. No other candidate reached the evidence bar; several plausible-looking leads are recorded as rejected/unconfirmed below. No code was executed; no runtime or browser confirmation was performed.
